fields.title: The Key Teachings of F. B. Meyer
fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of F. B. Meyer’s teaching — that the Christian’s power and peace lie in being where God would have him be, surrendered, Spirit-filled and walking daily with Christ, and that such a walk leads out into service among the poor. Fifteen short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as a companion to F. B. Meyer’s own public-domain works, which readers are warmly encouraged to go to directly.
fields.about_html:
This is not a book by F. B. Meyer. It is a companion to him — an independent work of exposition and appreciation, written by Ochorus, that gathers the heart of his teaching into fifteen short chapters for the ordinary reader, with an account of his life, a conclusion, and a guide to his books.

His teaching has a single thread. The believer who has handed the last key of his life to Christ may expect to be led, filled and kept — led by the three witnesses of God’s Word, the Spirit’s prompting and the unfolding of providence; filled with the Spirit not once but again and again; kept in a daily walk of quiet dependence; and sent out, as Meyer himself was sent, to prisoners and drunkards and the poor. Behind it all stands the Lord Jesus as our great High Priest, who has opened the way into the holiest. This volume follows that thread, weighs honestly the places where he must be read with care, and ends each chapter with a few questions and a prayer.

F. B. Meyer’s own writings are in the public domain and freely available, and every chapter here names the book it draws on so that the reader can go to the source. This companion is offered only to open the door to him. Scripture is quoted from the Authorised (King James) Version, and nothing here claims to stand in for his own warm, pictorial and searching pages.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore. PSALM 16:11

Frederick Brotherton Meyer was one of the best-loved preachers in the English-speaking world for the better part of fifty years, and almost nobody now remembers why. He wrote more than most men read. He preached, by the reckoning of his friends, many thousands of sermons, crossed the Atlantic again and again, spoke at the Keswick Convention for decades, and led two large London congregations. He was also, and this is the part that is easy to forget, a Baptist minister who met discharged prisoners at the gaol gate, campaigned against the drink trade and the brothels of South London, and was mocked for it.

He matters because he joined things that are usually kept apart. He was a man of the inner life who could not leave the slum alone. He was a teacher of surrender and the fulness of the Spirit who insisted on plain Bible study and sanctified common sense. He was a devotional writer, sometimes a sentimental one, who could also give a hard and searching account of why a Christian’s joy had dried up. And he wrote above all for the anxious, the slow and the ordinary, for people who were sure that God led everyone except them.

The one thread

If Meyer’s teaching can be put in a sentence, he put it himself on the first page of The Secret of Guidance: “so much of our power and peace consists in knowing where God would have us be, and in being just there.” Almost everything he wrote is an unfolding of that line. To be where God would have us be, the will must be surrendered. To know where that is, we must learn how God guides — by His Word, by the prompting of His Spirit, and by the slow unfolding of His providence. To stay there, we need the fulness of the Spirit, a daily walk with Christ, and a quiet heart. And being there will never mean staying comfortable. For Meyer, the God who led the soul into the secret place also led the hand into the back streets.

In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths. PROVERBS 3:6

Under that thread lies a foundation, and Meyer never let his readers forget it. We do not find our own way to God. The Lord Jesus, our great High Priest, has entered the holiest by His own blood and opened a new and living way for us to follow. Meyer’s exposition of Hebrews, The Way Into the Holiest, is the ground on which all his counsel about guidance and surrender stands. The surrendered life is not a ladder we climb; it is a door that has been opened, and we go in.

So the question to carry through these pages is simple. Not, how may I become a better Christian? but, am I where God would have me be, and have I given Him the last key?

How this book is arranged

After a chapter on his life, fifteen short chapters set out his teaching. The first group follows The Secret of Guidance: the three witnesses by which God leads, the waiting under the cloud, the surrendered will, the order of fact, faith and feeling, the indwelling Christ, and the fulness of the Spirit. The second group follows The Way Into the Holiest: the open way into God’s presence, the great High Priest, the gospel of rest, and the call to strip for the race. Among them come chapters on the still hour of the daily walk and on how to bear sorrow. The last group turns outward: to the Bible biographies for which he was best known, to his service among the poor and the prisoner, and to the temperance cause he pressed for most of his life. A conclusion and a reader’s guide close the book.

Each chapter ends with application points and a prayer. He would have wanted that. Nearly every reading in Our Daily Walk closes with a prayer, and he had no patience with religion that stayed in the notebook. Read a chapter at a time. Stop at the application points. Pray the prayer, or better, pray your own.

Where he must be read with care

This is not a book of hero-worship, and there are places where Meyer must be read with care. It is kinder to say so at the start.

First, Meyer belonged to the Keswick movement, and he sometimes spoke of the Christian life in two stages: a first coming to Christ for pardon, and a later, decisive handing over of the whole self, followed by a definite receiving of the Spirit’s fulness. Many sincere Christians have found that language freeing. Others, reading the same Scriptures, believe it divides believers into classes the New Testament does not recognise, and that it can leave the conscientious forever wondering whether they have had the experience. Meyer himself taught that the filling must be sought again and again, and he confessed that there was more in the doctrine than he understood. Chapters five and eight weigh this plainly.

Second, he was a Victorian devotional writer, and his style shows it. He piles picture on picture — harbours and steamships, crucibles and gardens — and some of his prose is more sentimental than a modern reader can bear. The substance underneath is usually sound and often searching.

Third, he was a Protestant controversialist of his day, and in The Way Into the Holiest he writes of Roman and Anglican priests in language that is sharp and, in places, uncharitable. His argument from Hebrews deserves a hearing. His tone does not need copying.

Fourth, he pressed total abstinence from alcohol as a Christian cause. His compassion for the victims of drink was real and costly, and he was right about the ruin it wrought in his generation. But Scripture does not forbid wine, and a rule wisely chosen for love’s sake must not be turned into a law binding every conscience. Chapter seventeen tries to honour his cause without making that mistake.

So the counsel of this book is the counsel of Scripture:

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21

Where he is faithful — on the finished work of Christ, on the surrendered will, on the sure guidance of a Father who stoops to the slowest child, on the need of the still hour, on the love that goes to the gaol gate — receive it gladly and put it into practice. Where he presses beyond what is written, mark it and set it aside. You will lose nothing. He would not have asked you to swallow him whole, and he would have been the first to send you from his pages back to the Bible.

A last word. Meyer was not a great theologian and never claimed to be. He was a pastor who wrote for people in counting-houses and sick-rooms. If this companion does anything, it should send you back to his own pages, and through them to the Lord he trusted to guide the perplexed.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Write down, honestly, the decision about which you most need God’s guidance at present. Keep the page; you will come back to it.

2. Ask yourself whether there is any part of your life — a habit, a relationship, an ambition — that you have not yet handed over to Christ.

3. Decide now how you will read: one chapter a day or a week, with a Bible open beside it.

4. Get hold of one of Meyer’s own books, in the Ochorus library or elsewhere, and read it alongside this one.

5. Name one person in need near you whom you have been avoiding. Pray for them by name as you begin.

A PRAYER
Lord, I want to be where You would have me be, and I confess I do not always want it enough to go there.
Show me the path of life. Take whatever I have kept back, and teach me to trust You with it.
Keep me from swallowing any teacher whole, and keep me from refusing any truth that comes from You.
And as I read, send me out to someone who needs me, for Your name’s sake. Amen.

fields.title: The Last Key
fields.body_html:
I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart. PSALM 40:8

A London boyhood. Frederick Brotherton Meyer was born in Clapham, then on the edge of London, on the eighth of April, 1847. His father was a prosperous City merchant of German descent, and the home was comfortable, cultured and devout. The family worshipped at Bloomsbury Chapel under the Baptist preacher William Brock, whose warm evangelical ministry and care for the poor of central London left a lasting mark on the boy. There was no dramatic conversion to tell of later, no rescue from the gutter. There was a steady early faith, baptism as a youth, and by his middle teens a settled sense that he was meant for the ministry. He went to school at Brighton College and then entered Regent’s Park College to train as a Baptist minister, taking his degree at the University of London.

A careful young minister. In 1870 he went to Liverpool as assistant to C. M. Birrell at Pembroke Chapel, one of the leading Baptist pulpits of the north, and there he learned the craft of a pastor from a gentle and cultivated master. In 1871 he married Jane Eliza Jones, who shared his life and work, and in 1872 he took his first charge of his own, at Priory Street Chapel in York. By his own later account he was at that stage correct, earnest and rather stiff: a good preacher of the orthodox kind, anxious about his reputation, and more at home with a manuscript than with a crowd.

Moody in York. In 1873 an unknown American evangelist arrived in York with a singer called Ira Sankey and very little in the way of introductions. Dwight L. Moody was a former shoe salesman with no theological training and not much grammar, and most of the ministers of the city kept their distance. Meyer did not. He opened his chapel to him, and in the weeks that followed he watched a man who spoke to God as to a friend and to sinners as to people he expected to see saved. It shook him. The two became friends for life, and Meyer always counted Moody among the great influences on his ministry: the man who taught him that preaching and practical work belong together, and that a minister’s business is not to be admired but to win people for Christ.

Leicester and the prison gate. In 1874 Meyer moved to Victoria Road Church in Leicester. It was a respectable congregation, and it did not care for the free methods and plain evangelism he had begun to learn. After some years of friction he resigned, and a new congregation gathered round him that became Melbourne Hall, a large and busy mission church in a working district of the town. There he began the practical work that marked the rest of his life. He is remembered for meeting men released from the Leicester gaol on the morning of their discharge, giving them breakfast, and helping them to find honest work — among other schemes, a small business chopping and selling firewood that gave them wages and a character to show an employer. Drunkards, the unemployed and the fallen found in Melbourne Hall a minister who expected them to be changed and who did not mind getting his hands dirty to help.

The surrender. It was in Leicester that the hour came which he spoke of for the rest of his life. In the mid-1880s a group of young Cambridge men, among them the cricketer C. T. Studd, were travelling the country before sailing for China, and some of them came to Leicester. Meyer was struck by something in them that he knew he lacked — an unhurried joy and an obvious ease with God. He asked them their secret, and the answer came back that they had given themselves to Christ entirely, holding nothing back. He went home and, as he told it many times afterwards, knelt and handed over his life to Christ as a man hands over a ring of keys, except for one small key he could not yet bring himself to give. The words he later taught others to pray were the words he prayed then. “If you are not willing, confess that you are willing to be made willing.” He found that Christ took him at his word. His preaching changed. His strained concern for himself eased. He began to speak of a Christ who lived within, and a Spirit who could be received by faith, and people who had heard him for years noticed the difference.

Keswick. From the late 1880s Meyer was a regular speaker at the Keswick Convention in the Lake District, the annual gathering for the deepening of the spiritual life that had grown out of the holiness meetings of the 1870s. He became one of its best-known voices, and he carried its message across the world. What he said there he said in his books: the surrendered will, the fulness of the Spirit, the life of faith rather than struggle, and the plain duty of obedience in the next small thing.

London. In 1888 he moved to Regent’s Park Chapel in London, and in 1892 to Christ Church, Westminster Bridge Road, in Lambeth, a great Congregational church south of the river founded by Newman Hall. There, in one of the poorest and roughest parts of London, he preached to large congregations on Sundays and on weekday afternoons, and led a sustained campaign against the public houses and brothels of the district. Opponents mocked him as a meddler; he went on. He returned to Regent’s Park for some years before the war and then to Christ Church once more, finally retiring from a pastorate of his own in his seventies. He served as President of the National Free Church Council and, in 1906, of the Baptist Union, and he did more than most men of his generation to make the Free Churches work together.

The pen and the road. Alongside the pulpit ran the pen. His Bible biographies — Abraham, Israel, Joseph, Moses, Joshua, Samuel, David, Elijah, Jeremiah, John the Baptist, Peter and Paul — sold in great numbers and are still read. His expositions of Hebrews, of the Shepherd Psalm and of the Gospel of John, his little books on the inner life, and his daily readings went all over the English-speaking world. He travelled as widely as he wrote. He crossed to America many times, preached in South Africa and far beyond, and took every invitation he could as long as his strength held. During the First World War he spoke up for conscientious objectors in prison when it was not a popular thing to do.

The end. He preached and wrote almost to the last. Early in 1929, in his eighty-second year, he was told that he had only days to live, and he is remembered for a note to a friend saying, in effect, that before it arrived he might have entered the palace, and that they would meet in the morning. He died on the twenty-eighth of March, 1929. He left no system and no denomination of his own. He left a shelf of books, a good many prisoners and drunkards who had found their feet, and a simple testimony that the man who gives Christ the last key does not lose his life but finds it.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Meyer was changed by an unknown evangelist whom most ministers kept at arm’s length. Whom are you holding at arm’s length who may have something to teach you?

2. He saw in a few young men a joy he did not have, and he asked them why. Is there someone whose walk with God you quietly envy? Ask them their secret.

3. Is there one key you are still keeping back from Christ? Name it to Him, even if you can only say that you are willing to be made willing.

4. Consider the prison gate. Is there a person leaving some kind of prison — addiction, disgrace, loneliness — whom you could meet with practical help this month?

5. Read the first chapter of The Secret of Guidance, in the Ochorus library, and notice how much of this life it explains.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You took a careful, anxious young minister and made him free. Do the same with me.
Here are the keys of my life. I cannot yet give You every one of them, but I am willing to be made willing.
Open the locked rooms, and fill them with Yourself.
And send me, as You sent Your servant, to the gaol gate and the back street, to those whom others pass by. Amen.

fields.title: The Secret of Guidance
fields.body_html:
I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye. PSALM 32:8

Meyer wrote many books, but the little collection of addresses called The Secret of Guidance is the one that has travelled furthest, and its title address is the reason. He wrote it for a particular kind of Christian: the one who believes that God guides His people, has read of Abraham and Moses and Paul being led, and quietly suspects that the guidance was meant for everyone except himself. And we must wait for God’s plan to unfold in providence. That is the fifth condition, and it brings us to the heart of his teaching.

The three witnesses

Meyer’s most famous contribution to the subject is a single sentence. “God’s impressions within and His word without are always corroborated by His Providence around, and we should quietly wait until these three focus into one point.” They have come to be known as the three lights, and a story is often told of Meyer learning the picture from a ship’s captain who brought his vessel into harbour at night by lining up three lamps on the shore. That story is not in the Ochorus text of the book, but the teaching is. There is the inward prompting of the Spirit. There is the written Word. And there is the outward arrangement of circumstances. When all three agree, he says, we may be as sure we are right as if an angel beckoned us on. When they do not, we should wait.

The strength of this is its balance. Each of the three, taken alone, can mislead. Inward impressions rise and fall with our health and our wishes; Meyer warns elsewhere that they often contradict one another. Circumstances can be read to mean almost anything by a mind already made up. And even Scripture can be wrenched from its context to prove what we want. But the Spirit does not contradict the Word He inspired, and the God who speaks in both is also the Lord of providence. Where the three line up, the danger of self-deception is much reduced.

In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established. 2 CORINTHIANS 13:1

It is worth adding a caution Meyer himself implies. The Word is not simply one witness among three. It is the test of the other two. No impression, however strong, and no open door, however wide, can make right what Scripture calls wrong. Meyer knew this; in the same book he warns sharply against those who magnify the inner light to the neglect of the Word, and calls it the prolific parent of all kinds of evil. His three witnesses work best when the reader keeps that order.

Only the next step

Meyer ends with a word for those who want to see the whole road before they will take a step. God, he says, does not promise that. “Not next year, but to-morrow. Not the next mile, but the next yard. Not the whole pattern, but the next stitch in the canvas.” Those who demand more will be disappointed and slip back into the dark. Those who take the next step find that the lights multiply as they go, like the lamps of a town seen from a night train.

He closes with a personal word: that after months of waiting and prayer he had become absolutely sure of his Father’s guidance, and wanted every troubled reader to wait patiently for the Lord until He made His will plain. It is the testimony of a man who had tried it.

1. Take the decision you wrote down at the start of this book. Examine your motive honestly: is your eye single, or is there some thought of your own advantage mixed in?

2. Ask yourself whether your will is surrendered in this matter. If not, tell God plainly that you are willing to be made willing.

3. Gather the facts. Write down what you know, what you need to find out, and what Scripture says that bears on it.

4. Pray this week that God will shut every door that is not His will, and then watch for what He shuts.

fields.title: Where the Cloud Rests
fields.body_html:
At the commandment of the LORD the children of Israel journeyed, and at the commandment of the LORD they pitched: as long as the cloud abode upon the tabernacle they rested in their tents. NUMBERS 9:18

Meyer called the ninth chapter of Numbers an exquisite picture-lesson on guidance, and he quoted the whole passage at the end of The Secret of Guidance as though nothing he could add would improve it. Over the tabernacle in the wilderness stood the cloud: a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night. When it lifted, Israel struck camp and followed. When it stayed, Israel stayed — whether for a night, or two days, or a month, or a year. They did not move because the pasture was poor or the view had grown dull. They did not stay because they were comfortable. They watched the cloud.

It is a lesson more about waiting than about moving, and that is why most of us find it hard.

Whether it were two days, or a month, or a year, that the cloud tarried upon the tabernacle, remaining thereon, the children of Israel abode in their tents, and journeyed not: but when it was taken up, they journeyed. NUMBERS 9:22

Stand still until you know

Meyer’s counsel on waiting is blunt. “If you do not know what you ought to do, stand still until you do.” He knew how hard that is. There are times, he says, when everyone insists that something must be done, when the Egyptians are behind, the cliffs on either hand, and the sea in front. It is not easy then to stand still and see the salvation of God. But we must.

His warning example is Saul. Samuel had told the king to wait for him at Gilgal, and when the prophet seemed late and the people were slipping away, Saul forced himself and offered the sacrifice. Meyer calls it the great mistake of his life. Saul did not lack zeal or courage. He lacked the patience to let God come in God’s time, and he acted rather than be seen to do nothing.

Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will shew to you to day. EXODUS 14:13

There is a practical side to this that Meyer spells out in his address on burdens. If you are not sure of God’s will, he says, it is a good way in dealing with Him to tell Him you will stay where you are, or go on doing what you have been doing, until He makes quite clear what He wants and gives you the power to do it. That is not laziness. It is putting the responsibility for change on God, and trusting Him to make any alteration plain enough that even a dull servant cannot miss it.

God’s delays

The hardest part of waiting is that God seems slow. Meyer does not pretend otherwise. There was delay, he writes, before Sennacherib’s army lay dead round Jerusalem; delay before Jesus came walking on the sea in the fourth watch; delay before He came to Bethany, and before the angel woke Peter on the night before his execution. God stays long enough to test the patience of faith, but never a moment beyond the hour of real need.

For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry. HABAKKUK 2:3

In Our Daily Walk he returns to the theme under a title that has become a proverb: “God’s delays are not denials.” He points to the angel at the Jabbok, who waited until Jacob could wrestle no more before He blessed him; to the Syrophenician woman, whom Jesus answered only when she fell at His feet; to Lazarus, whom He let die. In every case, Meyer says, God was not neglectful but waiting, at no small cost to His own heart, until we had come to the end of ourselves and He could do more than we had dared to ask.

And therefore will the LORD wait, that he may be gracious unto you, and therefore will he be exalted, that he may have mercy upon you: for the LORD is a God of judgment: blessed are all they that wait for him. ISAIAH 30:18

This is a comfort, and it is also a searching. Much of what we call waiting on God is really waiting for God to agree with us. Meyer’s waiting is different. It is the waiting of a will that has already said yes and only wants to know where.

The shut door

Waiting is not always a matter of sitting still. Sometimes God guides by closing. Meyer’s favourite example is Paul’s second journey, when the apostle tried to go into Asia and was forbidden, then tried Bithynia, and the Spirit suffered them not (Acts 16:7). The little band found themselves at Troas, facing the sea, with nowhere left to go. That night came the vision of the man of Macedonia.

After they were come to Mysia, they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not. ACTS 16:7

“The Spirit of Jesus often shuts doors in the long corridors of life,” he writes in Our Daily Walk. We walk along trying one after another, and they are locked, so that we may come to the one He has opened. And the open door may be small. When Paul reached Philippi he found no crowd, only a few women at a place of prayer by the river. But one of them was Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened, and a church began. “A small door may lead to a vast opportunity.” The lesson is not to despise the one door left open because it looks too narrow for our hopes.

When it is time to move

It would be easy to turn all this into a charter for indecision, and Meyer did not intend that. The same book that says stand still says also that God usually speaks through deliberate thought, weighing the reasons for and against. In Our Daily Walk he is plainer still. Where our judgement can reach a right conclusion, he says, we are left to think the matter out; use the materials within reach, balance them, look to God to keep you from mistake, and act. And once you have decided in faith and prayer, go forward, not doubting or looking back.

And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left. ISAIAH 30:21

So there is a time to wait and a time to walk, and the wise Christian needs both. Meyer’s rule of thumb is simple: when the three witnesses agree, move; when they do not, wait; and in the meantime do faithfully the duty that lies in front of you. The cloud that rests over the tent today will lift tomorrow, and the manna will be on the ground wherever it next comes down.

Leaving the plan with Him

Underneath all his counsel on waiting lies a single conviction: the government of our lives is on Christ’s shoulder, not ours. “Put the government of your life upon His shoulder, and leave Him to execute His plan,” he writes. Do not get anxious or flurried. Tell Him, if need be, that you will stand still until He puts His arms under you and carries you where He would have you be.

Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass. PSALM 37:5

That is not the counsel of a man who never had to wait. It is the counsel of a man who had learned, often slowly, that God’s pace is not ours and is better.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Is there a matter in which you are pressing ahead because waiting feels like failure? Consider Saul at Gilgal, and ask whether you need to stop.

2. Try Meyer’s practical rule: tell God you will go on as you are until He makes a change plain. Then do today’s duty faithfully.

3. Think of a door God has shut in your life. Can you now see anything He opened because of it?

4. Look for the small door. Is there a modest opportunity in front of you that you have despised because it seemed too little?

5. Where your judgement can decide, stop waiting for a sign. Weigh the matter, pray, decide, and go forward.

A PRAYER
Lord, You lead Your people by a cloud that does not move to our timetable. Teach me to watch it.
When I must wait, give me patience; when You delay, keep me from thinking You have forgotten.
Shut the doors You do not want me to enter, and give me eyes to see the small door You have opened.
And when it is time to move, give me courage to go forward without looking back. Amen.

fields.title: Willing to Be Made Willing
fields.body_html:
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. ROMANS 12:1

Every movement has its keyword, and the keyword of the Keswick Convention, where Meyer spoke for so many years, was consecration. It meant the definite handing over of the whole self to Christ as Lord: not merely trusting Him for pardon, but giving Him the house and all its keys. Meyer had come to it himself in Leicester, and he never stopped pressing it on others. In The Secret of Guidance he puts it plainly: “Consecration is the indispensable condition of blessedness.”

Saviour and King

fields.title: Fact, Faith, Feeling
fields.body_html:
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. ROMANS 5:1

Three words stand at the head of one of Meyer’s shortest addresses, and they have probably helped more anxious Christians than anything else he wrote. Fact. Faith. Feeling. The trouble with most of us, he says, is not that we lack any of the three but that we put them in the wrong order. “We say, feeling, faith, fact. God says fact, faith, feeling.”

We want to feel forgiven before we believe we are forgiven, and to believe before we have looked at what God has done. It is like trying to build the top storey of a house before the foundations. Meyer’s order is the reverse, and he set it out in three lines: “God’s Facts, laid like a foundation of adamant. Our Faith, apprehending and resting on them.” And last, joyous feelings, which may come at once or after days and months, as God wills.

The facts first

The facts, Meyer says, are like stepping-stones across a brook. From a distance you cannot see how to cross. It is no use consulting your feelings about it from the bank. You must come down to the water, look at the stones, see how firmly they are set, and step.

He lists some of them. God loves each of us with a tender and particular love. In Christ every obstacle to our forgiveness has been removed. The one who trusts Christ is born into God’s family and is a child, whether he feels like one or not. God takes what we give Him as soon as we give it. In Christ we are seated in the heavenly places. There is a share in the gift of Pentecost waiting for every member of Christ.

Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. PHILIPPIANS 1:6

None of these depends on how we feel. Meyer tells of soldiers hiding in the woods after the American Civil War, starving on berries long after peace had been signed, because they had not heard or did not believe the news. Their unbelief cost them dearly. It did not undo the peace.

Standing and experience

In the address called Where Am I Wrong? he draws the same line in different words. Many Christians, he says, confuse their standing with their experience. Experience is as changeable as April weather, sun and cloud chasing each other across the moor. Standing does not change, because it did not begin with us, was not bought by us, and is not kept by us.

He puts it in a picture from the world of money that his hearers would have understood at once. “Our standing in Jesus is our invested capital. Our emotions at the best are but our spending money,” always passing through our pockets and never quite the same. The heir’s fortune does not rise and fall with the coins in his purse.

Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. HEBREWS 13:8

Living in the will

If feelings do not settle our standing, what does God look for in us? Meyer’s answer is the will. We cannot command our feelings, but we can direct our wills. “In His sight we are not what we feel, but what we will.” So he counsels his readers to live not in the summer-house of emotion but in the central citadel of the will.

He gives an example every Christian will recognise. At the Lord’s Table the heart is full, and every part of us joins in praise. Next morning it is the counting-house or the factory, and the glow has gone, and we wonder whether we were ever as devoted as we thought. Meyer’s counsel is to look up and tell God that though the tide of feeling has gone out, the will has not moved a hair’s breadth: we are as much His as we were at the Table. That, he says, is an offering God is pleased with.

Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established. PROVERBS 16:3

Faith that looks away

What of faith itself? Here Meyer is at his most helpful. If you want a true faith, he says, do not think about your faith; look at the facts, and at the Person they concern. We rest not on the atonement but on Him who made it; not on the resurrection but on Him who rose. And when the anxious ask whether they have the right kind of faith, he gives them one of his best sentences: “All faith that turns towards Jesus is the right faith.” It may be as weak as the woman’s touch on the hem of His garment, or as desperate as Peter’s cry as he sank. If it turns to Christ, it is enough.

And Jesus answering saith unto them, Have faith in God. MARK 11:22

He learned, he says, to stop measuring his faith by God’s greatness and to lean it instead on God’s faithfulness. In dark hours of nervous depression he had gone to God and said that his faith was flickering out, but that God was faithful and he was reckoning on Him. “Do not trouble about your Faith; reckon on God’s Faithfulness.”

Feeling in its place

None of this makes Meyer an enemy of feeling. As a rule, he says, faith fruits in feeling; the prodigal came home to music and dancing. Joy is a fruit of the Spirit. But the lack of it does not always mean something is wrong. Our feelings are affected by our health, the weather, and whether we slept well, and God knows it. When Elijah lay under the juniper tree and asked to die, God did not rebuke him; He sent him sleep and food.

Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God. PSALM 42:11

Meyer also noticed that temperaments differ. Some people, he writes, seem born in the dark, their nature set in a minor key. They may never have the bright gladness others have, and they must not blame themselves for it. But there may still be rest, victory and serenity.

Where he must be read with care

Meyer’s counsel is wise, but one strand needs balancing. In the same address he urges his readers to be indifferent to emotion, and even, when they suffer, to give no sign of it, lest they be a stumbling-block to others. That can be heard as a counsel of pretence, and it has sometimes been used to make the grieving or depressed hide what they ought to bring into the open. The Psalms do not hide their tears, and Meyer himself, writing on sorrow, insists that tears are natural and that Jesus wept. Put the facts first, by all means, and do not live by feelings. But do not pretend to feelings you do not have, and do not despise the ones you do.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Write down three facts about your standing in Christ that do not depend on how you feel. Read them aloud each morning this week.

2. Notice the next time your feelings dip after a spiritual high. Tell God that your will has not moved.

3. Stop examining your faith for a week. Each time you are tempted to, look instead at one promise of God and reckon on His faithfulness.

4. If you are of a sombre temperament, stop measuring yourself by others’ gladness. Ask God for rest and serenity instead.

5. Is there a grief or darkness you have been hiding from those who love you? Consider telling one trusted friend.

A PRAYER
Father, I have tried to feel my way to You, and I have sunk every time.
Set my feet on the facts: that You love me, that Christ has died and risen, that I am Your child.
When my feelings fail, keep my will fixed on You. When my faith flickers, let me lean on Your faithfulness.
And give me, in Your own time, the joy that follows faith. Amen.

fields.title: Christ in You
fields.body_html:
To whom God would make known what is the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles; which is Christ in you, the hope of glory. COLOSSIANS 1:27

Meyer opens the third address in The Secret of Guidance by remarking how fitting it is that the largest church in London should be dedicated to the apostle Paul. Gentiles owe Paul a great debt, for it was to him that God unveiled two mysteries that touch us especially. The first was that Gentiles need not become Jews in order to become Christians. The second, which Meyer thought the Church had hardly begun to grasp, was that the Lord Jesus is willing to dwell within a Gentile heart. That He should live in a child of Abraham was wonder enough. That He should make His home in us was, to the first believers, almost incredible.

Meyer called this the secret of Christ’s indwelling, and he thought it was the hinge of the Christian life.

The mystery

His statement of it is bare: “Christ is in the believer.” Not because we are good, he says, or because we are trying hard to be wholehearted, or because we keep Him there by the strength of our love, but because we believe, and in believing have thrown open the doors and windows of our nature. And He has come in.

That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love, may be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height. EPHESIANS 3:17–18

He adds a word for those who cannot remember when it happened. Christ comes quietly, Meyer says, without a footfall in the passage, His step so light that it does not break a bruised reed. “Do not be surprised, therefore, if you cannot tell the day or the hour when the Son of Man came to dwell within you. Only know that He has come.” It is a kind word for Christians who have never had a dramatic experience and have been made to feel second-rate for it.

Why we do not notice Him

If Christ is really within, why are so many believers unaware of Him? Meyer’s answer is that He dwells deep. Below the life of the body, below the busy life of thought and feeling and imagination, in the deepest place of the spirit, Christ lives by His Spirit as the glory once dwelt behind the veil in the most holy place, hidden from view. And most of us seldom go down so far. We eat and drink and work and read, make short trips into questions of right and wrong, and live almost entirely on the surface.

Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you? 1 CORINTHIANS 3:16

The remedy is not to try to feel Him. Here Meyer applies his rule of fact, faith and feeling. He confesses frankly that he does not always feel Christ there; amid temptation or storm he often cannot see His form or hear His voice. But he dares to believe He is there, not as a guest for a night but as a permanent resident, unchanged by our changes. It is a medieval tale and should be taken as an illustration, not a revelation. But the point is sound and pastoral: the very pain we feel at our temptations may be a sign that Christ is within, not that He has gone.

The riches of the glory

Paul speaks not only of the mystery but of the riches of its glory, and Meyer delights in the phrase. If all the treasures of wisdom and grace are in Christ, and Christ is in us, then we are rich. “It is like a poor man having a millionaire friend come to live with him.”

He names two of these riches. The first is patience. Life, he says, is not easy for anyone; no branch escapes the knife, no jewel the wheel. People vex us beyond bearing, and the pace of modern life frays our nerves. And he lists what patience would really mean — never to relax the watch on ourselves, never to speak the hasty word, to be more thoughtful of others than of ourselves, to drink the bitter cup without complaining — and admits that no mere stoicism could give it. But the patience of the Lamb who was dumb before His shearers is ours, because He is in us.

The second is grace for every demand. Here Meyer gives a piece of advice that is worth more than many books. Meyer ends with three pieces of counsel, and they are more demanding than the rest of the address. First, be still each day for a little while before God, and ask the Spirit to show you the truth of Christ’s indwelling. Second, reverence your body and soul as His temple, and let Him drive out what does not belong there, as He once cleared the temple courts. Third, hate your own life — by which Meyer means the self-life, with its restless striving after independence and its own way. fields.body_html:
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit. EPHESIANS 5:18

The last address in The Secret of Guidance takes as its text four words from Ephesians, and it opens with a sentence that sums up the burden of Meyer’s ministry after Leicester: “Nothing can compensate the Church, or the individual Christian, for the lack of the Holy Spirit.” What a full stream is to a mill-wheel, he says, the Spirit is to the Church. Without Him we stand powerless before our difficulties and our enemies, however good our organisation or our preaching.

A thread or a river

Meyer is careful not to say that ordinary Christians have no Spirit. If they had none, he says, they would not be Christians at all. But in many of us He is present only as a thin thread, a silver streak, a shallow brook. Why, he asks, should we be content with that?

He traces the want of the Spirit in four common complaints. Do you lack assurance, happy one day and troubled the next? It is the Spirit who witnesses with our spirit that we are children of God. Do you lack victory over sin? The Spirit lusts against the flesh, and sin can no more stand before Him than darkness before the morning. Do you lack the fruits of holiness, the tender and unselfish spirit you see in others? It is the Spirit’s fruit, not ours. Do you lack power in service? It was when the first Christians were filled with the Holy Ghost that they spoke the word with boldness.

And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness. ACTS 4:31

For all, not for a few

Meyer insisted that the fulness is not the privilege of an elite. Before Pentecost, he says, the fulness of the Spirit was given to the few — to an Elijah, an Isaiah, a Daniel. Since Pentecost it has been poured out on the many: on women and children, obscure thinkers, hidden workers, servants and handmaids. He takes Peter’s words at Pentecost as the charter of every believer’s claim.

For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call. ACTS 2:39

And he makes a striking argument from the form of the text. Be filled with the Spirit is a command, as plain as the command on the same page that husbands love their wives. We obey it at our peril. But Meyer adds, “all God’s commands are enablings.” He never tells us to become what He is not prepared to make us.

Five conditions

As with guidance, Meyer sets out conditions for receiving the Spirit’s fulness. They are worth hearing, because they protect the teaching from its dangers.

There must be desire. God does not give this gift to those who are content without it. Meyer suggests reading the Acts of the Apostles to stir the desire up, and the lives of men like Brainerd, Martyn and McCheyne.

The motive must be right. Here Meyer is at his sharpest. If we want the Spirit in order to have a certain experience, or to draw people to ourselves, or to be happy, we will probably be disappointed. “God will not find water for us to use for turning our own water-wheels.” The Spirit’s one passion is the glory of Christ, and He will fill only those who share it.

He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you. JOHN 16:14

Scripture must be honoured. This is one of the most important things Meyer ever said, and it is the best guard against the excesses that have often attended teaching on the Spirit. Some, he warns, have so magnified the inner light that they have neglected the Word, and this is the parent of all kinds of evil, because then we have no test for the voices within. “We must not be content with the Spirit without the Word, or with the Word without the Spirit.” The Word is the Spirit’s chosen instrument, and the two run together like the two rails of a line.

The Spirit must be allowed to do as He will. That means daily obedience, and the painful business of letting the self-life decrease while Christ increases. A look, a word, a refusal can grieve Him. Meyer does not soften this, but he adds that the Spirit is the Spirit of love, and will ask nothing without a reason we would approve if we knew what He knows.

And the gift must be received by faith. As we received Christ, so we receive the Spirit’s fulness: ask, then take, then rise and go on reckoning that God has kept His word. There may be no rushing wind and no tongue of fire. Do not look for them, Meyer says; “believe, in spite of feeling, that you are filled.” The feeling will come in its time, and the fruit will begin to show.

If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him? LUKE 11:13

Not once for all

The sixth point of the address is perhaps the most valuable, and it corrects the danger in all the others. It is not enough, Meyer says, to be filled once for all. The apostles who were filled in the second chapter of Acts were filled again in the fourth. So he urges his readers to seek a fresh filling every morning, and again whenever they are aware of leakage — after exhausting service, or when some new duty or new temptation opens up. “Happy is that man who never leaves his chamber in the morning without definitely seeking and receiving the plenitude of the Spirit!”

He even finds three tenses in Acts. There is filled, a sudden decisive experience for a particular work. There is were being filled, as though the process were always going on. And there is full, the settled condition of a man like Stephen.

And the disciples were filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost. ACTS 13:52

Reading him with care

Meyer was a leading voice of Keswick, and teaching like this has been read in two quite different ways. Some have taken it as a call to one great crisis after conversion that settles the matter, a baptism of the Spirit that divides Christians into two classes. Later Pentecostal movements took up his language of enduement and baptism of fire and ran with it in directions he did not go; he himself thought the special gifts of the apostolic age had been withdrawn, though he wondered aloud whether the Church’s unfaithfulness was partly to blame.

The best reading of Meyer is his own sixth point. The fulness of the Spirit is not a trophy won once but a daily dependence, sought again and again, tested by the Word and shown in fruit and in Christ-exalting service. And he closed the address with a humility that should disarm anyone tempted to make his words a system: there was more in the doctrine, he said, than he had grasped, and “The fiery baptism of the Holy Spirit may be something far beyond.”

But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. GALATIANS 5:22–23
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Which of Meyer’s four complaints — lack of assurance, victory, fruit or power — describes you most? Bring it to God by name.

2. Examine your motive. Why do you want more of the Spirit? For His glory or for your experience?

3. Begin tomorrow morning, before you leave your room, by asking to be filled afresh, and then thank God that He has kept His word.

4. Keep the Word and the Spirit together: read a passage of Scripture before you pray for guidance or power.

5. Is there a small disobedience that may be grieving the Spirit? Deal with it today.

A PRAYER
Holy Spirit, I have lived on a thread when You meant me to have a river.
Fill me, not for my own comfort or name, but that Christ may be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death.
Keep me close to the Word You gave, and make me obedient in the least things.
Fill me today, and again tomorrow, and every day until I see Him. Amen.

fields.title: The Way into the Holiest
fields.body_html:
Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh. HEBREWS 10:19–20

Behind all Meyer’s practical counsel on guidance and surrender stands a book that many of his readers never opened: The Way Into the Holiest, his chapter-by-chapter exposition of the Epistle to the Hebrews. It is the most doctrinal thing of his in the Ochorus library, and it is the foundation of the rest. A man cannot talk long about the surrendered life, the indwelling Christ and the fulness of the Spirit without being asked on what ground a sinner may come near to God at all. Hebrews is Meyer’s answer.

Shadows and realities

In his short preface Meyer names two tendencies of his day that the epistle corrects. One was a readiness to play down the substitutionary side of Christ’s death, to treat the cross as example or inspiration rather than sacrifice. The other was a readiness to make too much of outward rite and ceremony. Hebrews, he says, answers both. It teaches that our Lord’s death was a sacrifice, and it teaches that we have passed from the realm of shadows into that of realities.

For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us. HEBREWS 9:24

He had a high view of the Old Testament ceremonies because of this. He calls the Book of Leviticus the seed-plot of New Testament theology, and he urges his readers not to turn from it lightly. The tabernacle, its furniture and its sacrifices were pictures, he says, and sometimes a picture shows detail we would miss in the dazzle of the thing itself. But they were only pictures. The Jews had the shadow; we have the substance. They had the example; we have the reality.

The veil and the holiest

In the tabernacle, and later the temple, the most holy place stood behind a heavy veil. Only one man might enter, the high priest, and only on one day of the year, and never without blood. The veil said, as plainly as cloth could say it, that the way into God’s presence was not yet open.

And the LORD said unto Moses, Speak unto Aaron thy brother, that he come not at all times into the holy place within the vail before the mercy seat, which is upon the ark; that he die not. LEVITICUS 16:2

Then Christ died, and the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom. Meyer reads it as God’s own announcement that the way was now open, without let or hindrance, to every trembling seeker. What that means for the believer he puts in a sentence of great simplicity: “We may go continually, and even dwell, where Israel’s high priests might tread but once each year.” The holiest place, he says, was the chamber of innermost communion with God. To enter it now is to make God our confidant and friend, into whose ear we may pour the whole story of our sin and sorrow and need.

And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom. MATTHEW 27:51

New and living

Meyer lingers over the two adjectives the epistle gives the way. It is living because it is not a road but a Person. We come to God through the living Saviour, and no one comes to the Father but by Him. And it is new, which Meyer takes to mean not merely recent but perpetually fresh: “It is new, because, though myriads have trodden it, it is as fresh as ever for each new priestly foot.” The veil, the epistle says, was His flesh. We come near to God through the real death of a real man, who hung on the cross in real human sorrow.

This matters for the rest of his teaching. When Meyer speaks elsewhere of the secret place of God’s presence, he is careful to say that no one can have a glad consciousness of God except through Jesus. Apart from Christ, he writes in The Secret of Guidance, the presence of God is an object of terror. In Christ, every barrier is down and every veil torn.

The blood that speaks

The Way Into the Holiest does not shrink from the language of blood, and Meyer defends it hotly. It is the only word, he says, that gathers up all that the death of Christ means: life, life poured out, life poured out violently, life poured out as a sacrifice. And he refuses the suggestion that the cross was only a noble martyrdom. Christ died not as a martyr, but as a Saviour.

fields.title: A Great High Priest
fields.body_html:
Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession. HEBREWS 4:14

There is a craving deep in the human heart, Meyer says in The Way Into the Holiest, that wit and sarcasm have never been able to kill: the craving for a priest. Someone to stand between us and God, to lay one hand on each and bring them together. Every people has built its altars and set apart its priests. Israel had the sons of Aaron, and for centuries the whole life of the nation was bound up with them. And the Hebrew Christians to whom the epistle was written had given all that up for a faith with no visible temple, no ceremony and no priest in robes. It must have felt, Meyer says, like a great privation.

The epistle’s answer is that they had not lost a priest. They had gained the only true one.

Priests need a Priest

Meyer is plain about our need. It is the conscious sinner, he says, who needs the Priest. We can manage very well with Christ as teacher or example or ideal man, until we see ourselves as God sees us; then we cry out for someone who can stand for us with God. And he is equally plain that this need does not end at conversion. Believers are made priests unto God, to offer prayer and praise and surrendered lives. But our tears need cleansing, our holiest hours need His merit, and our best service would condemn us without His sacrifice. “Priests need a Priest.”

Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people. HEBREWS 2:17

He adds a word to preachers that has not lost its point. Light views of sin, he warns, produce light views of the cross. If preachers would lay aside their literary essays and their clever arguments and deal with sin as sin, their hearers would feel their need of the Priest again, and there would be a return of old-fashioned conversions.

Touched with the feeling of our infirmities

The High Priest of Hebrews is not remote. He has passed through the heavens, as the high priest of old passed through the veil, carrying the blood of His own sacrifice into the presence of God. But He has not left our nature behind.

For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. HEBREWS 4:15

Meyer draws out the tenderness of this. Every avenue by which temptation reaches us — the eye, the ear, the imagination — was used against Christ, and He never gave way. And all His experiences, Meyer says, are present to Him still. When we come to Him for mercy or help, He knows at once how much we need and where. He compares Christ’s sympathy to the nervous system of a body: every thrill of pain in the smallest member runs at once to the heart, and help comes back as fast. “Oh to live in touch with Christ!” he exclaims, always touching Him as the woman touched the hem of His garment, and receiving the answer.

Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need. HEBREWS 4:16

Of that last verse he makes a whole chapter. Every hour, he says, is a time of need, and we are safest when we feel it most. We need mercy at our worst and at our best, and help for the valleys and the heights. And the throne we approach is not the great white throne of judgement but the rainbow-circled throne of grace. To the soul that says it dare not go, or dare not go as often as it needs, or dare not ask for small things, Meyer answers: you may come as often and as boldly as you will.

After the order of Melchizedek

In chapter seven of Hebrews the argument turns to the mysterious figure of Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the most high God, who met Abraham with bread and wine and blessed him. Meyer follows the epistle’s reasoning with evident enjoyment. Abraham gave him tithes, and the lesser is blessed by the greater, so Melchizedek stood above Abraham, and therefore above Levi and Aaron, who were yet in Abraham’s loins. If the old priesthood had been enough, why did David’s psalm promise another priest of a different order?

The LORD hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. PSALM 110:4

Meyer notices something about Melchizedek that he plainly loved. He was a priest outside the covenant people, who took tithes of a man of another race and blessed him. Meyer calls this a large-hearted view of priesthood that deals with man as man, and sees in it a picture of Christ, whose priesthood leaps every boundary of nation and birth. Then he names what makes Christ the greatest of high priests: He was appointed by the oath of God, He continues for ever in the power of an endless life, His character is blameless, and His person is divine.

To the uttermost

The chapter builds to one of the great promises of the New Testament.

Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them. HEBREWS 7:25

Meyer writes of it for those who are near despair, whose past seems too black to be forgiven and whose old habits laugh at every resolution. His answer is one of his finest sentences: “the greatness of our sin is always less than the greatness of God’s grace.” Deeper than the depths of our need is the mercy of God. And to those who were troubled in his day by questions about the clean heart and how far a Christian may be delivered from sin, he gave advice that deserves to be remembered: “Cease to think of cleansing, and consider the Cleanser.” Look away from the theory of deliverance to the Deliverer. So long as He is in possession, sin will lose its power.

Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us. ROMANS 8:34

Reading him with care

The Way Into the Holiest is a Protestant book written in a combative age, and in this part of it Meyer turns on the priests of the Roman and Anglican churches in language that is scornful and, frankly, unkind. His argument has a point: Hebrews does teach that Christ’s priesthood is unique and that no other mediator of sacrifice or absolution is needed. But a reader today can hold that conviction without his contempt for those who disagree. Christ the High Priest, touched with the feeling of our infirmities, is not honoured by a lack of feeling for others.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Do you feel your need of a Priest, or do you manage well enough with Christ as teacher and example? Ask God to show you your sin as He sees it.

2. Name a temptation you face often. Bring it to the High Priest who was tempted in the same way, and ask for help in time of need.

3. Go to the throne of grace today for something small that you would normally not bother God with.

4. If your past troubles you, read Hebrews 7:25 aloud, and say Meyer’s sentence after it: my sin is less than His grace.

5. Examine how you speak of Christians of other traditions. Does your tone honour the High Priest who is touched with our infirmities?

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, great High Priest, You have passed into the heavens and You have not forgotten what it is to be tempted.
I come boldly to Your throne of grace, not because I am worthy, but because You bid me come.
Save me to the uttermost, and keep interceding for me when I do not know how to pray.
Keep me always in touch with You, as close as the hand on the hem of Your garment. Amen.

fields.title: The Gospel of Rest
fields.body_html:
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his. HEBREWS 4:9–10

Meyer’s chapter on the fourth chapter of Hebrews begins with a description of his own age that could have been written yesterday. Strong and useful workers, he says, are breaking down early under the strain of mental toil. The brain was never made to bear such wear. And yet it is not that we work so much harder than our grandparents did, but that there is so much more fret and chafe and worry in our lives. Competition is closer, the pace is faster, and the age seems merciless to anyone who stumbles. We could stand the work, he says, if only we had rest from the worry. Is such a rest possible?

The epistle says it is, and Meyer calls its message the Gospel of Rest.

God’s rest

The rest the epistle offers is God’s own rest — the rest into which He entered on the seventh day. Meyer notices that Genesis gives no evening and morning for that day, as it does for the others, and he takes it as a hint that God’s rest has no end; that all the ages of human history are hours within it; and that we are invited not just to watch it but to share it, as a child may dip its cup into a great lake and drink without making a ripple.

And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. GENESIS 2:2

What kind of rest is it? Not the rest of weariness, for God does not faint. Not the rest of idleness, for Jesus said His Father was still working. It was the rest of a finished work, the satisfaction of One who looked at what He had made and saw that it was very good. So the rest offered to us is not slumber or indolence, but, in Meyer’s phrase, “the rest which is possible amid swift activity and strenuous work”: a contented heart, a will at peace with God’s will, and depths that the storms on the surface do not reach.

Christ has entered it for us

Neither the Sabbath nor Canaan exhausted that rest, the epistle argues; long after Joshua, David was still speaking of a rest to come. But there is a further reason for confidence. Jesus, our forerunner, has entered it. As God rested after creation, Christ rested after redemption. He lay in the tomb on the seventh day, Meyer says, not because He was exhausted but because the work was finished and there was nothing left to do. Then He sat down at the right hand of God. And because we are united to Him, we have entered the rest in Him and have only to take hold of it by faith.

For we which have believed do enter into rest. HEBREWS 4:3

Four ways into the rest

Meyer then becomes practical, as he always does, and gives four ways in which the rest is actually enjoyed.

First, we must will the will of God. So long as God’s will goes one way and ours another, there can be no rest, any more than in a house where the children are always fighting their parents. God’s will is going to be done. If we resist it, the yoke only rubs a sore place. The one who learns to say a perpetual yes to it — even so, Father — finds rest for his soul.

Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. MATTHEW 11:29

Second, we must accept the finished work of Christ. Many believers live as though they still had to do something — by tears or prayers or good works — to make themselves acceptable. “Why should we try to add one stitch to a finished garment,” Meyer asks, or one stroke to a pardon already signed and sealed? What satisfies Christ may well satisfy us.

Third, we must trust our Father’s care. Here Meyer lists the cares that crowd in on us — fear of poverty, household and business cares, cares about servants and children and money, cares like a swarm of gnats on a summer evening — and says that the secret is to learn the habit of handing each one over to God the moment its shadow falls, and to accept even interruptions and insults as permitted by Him.

Fourth, we must follow the Shepherd. The mountain track is often lost in mist. But the Guide knows the way, and walks unseen beside us, whispering peace.

Burdens, and what to do with them

In The Secret of Guidance Meyer returns to the same theme in an address on burdens, and he begins with the Sabbath. The law forbade Israel to carry burdens through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. The outward rule, he says, was a picture of an inward rest that is meant for every day. And the secret of that rest is not to carry burdens into it. “Care will break the rest of the soul as much as sin does.”

Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you. 1 PETER 5:7

He makes a distinction that keeps this teaching from being cruel. There is a difference, he says, between care and pain — between the self-made burden of anxiety and the suffering God sends to teach us. The second must not be made light of. But the first we are not meant to carry. And he adds a sentence that goes to the root of much Christian exhaustion: “God is pledged to give strength for all duties which He sets, but not for the burdens which we elect to take on as well.”

He names the burdens that earnest Christians most often carry needlessly. The burden of how to grow in grace: we may leave our progress to the Teacher, as a child leaves his promotion to the school. The burden of keeping up a Christian profession: He who saved can keep. The burden of Christian work, of which Meyer knew a good deal: how to keep the congregation, how to find sermons, how to hold our ground. “They could bear the work, but not the worry.” The work is His, and He bears the world in His arms as a mother holds a sick child. And the burden of our changing feelings, which we may hand over to Him who remembers that we are dust.

The remedy for them all is the same. Kneel down, Meyer says, and deliberately hand each burden to Jesus as once you handed Him your sins. Say, Lord, I entrust this to You; I cannot carry it; take it, and give me Your peace.

Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus. PHILIPPIANS 4:6–7

Reading him with care

One line in the address needs care. fields.title: The Still Hour
fields.body_html:
My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up. PSALM 5:3

Meyer was one of the busiest men of his generation. He ran a large church and a web of missions, preached several times a week, travelled constantly and wrote books at a rate that still astonishes. And the counsel he gave more often than any other was to stop. Be still. Shut the door. Take time. His generation spoke of the morning watch, the quiet time at the start of the day before its business begins, and Meyer pressed it on his hearers because he knew how easily a busy Christian loses it.

The neglect of the still hour

In Where Am I Wrong?, the address in which he diagnoses the loss of Christian joy, one of the causes he names is simply this: too little time alone with God through His Word. It is not necessary, he says, to make long prayers. But it is essential to be much alone with God. And then comes a sentence that every active Christian should hang on the wall: “No number of meetings, no fellowship with Christian friends, no amount of Christian activity can compensate for the neglect of the still hour.”

But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly. MATTHEW 6:6

He knew the difficulty. We do not always want to pray. His counsel is blunt and kind together: “When you feel least inclined for it, there is most need to make for your closet with the shut door.” Do for duty’s sake, he says, what you cannot yet do for pleasure, and it will become a delight. When you cannot pray for yourself, pray for others. When desire flags, take a text and turn it into a petition, or count your mercies and turn each into praise. And if the Bible itself has become dull, ask whether you have spoiled your appetite with sweets.

The Word first

For Meyer the still hour was always a Bible hour. He did not mean a hurried verse and a prayer, but real reading. He looked for a widespread revival of private Bible study, and said there was no short and easy method of godliness that could do without it. In Our Daily Walk he gives a homely piece of advice about the order of things: “Let us each one resolve to soak ourselves in the Scripture before turning to prayer,” as water poured into a pump helps to draw water up.

Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. PSALM 119:105

He practised a way of meditating that many have found helpful. There is no better way of communing with God, he writes, than to walk up and down in your room or in the open air, Bible in hand, turning its precepts and promises into prayer. God walks in the glades of Scripture, as once in the garden in the cool of the day.

The first words of the day

Meyer’s own habit at waking is recorded in the first reading of Our Daily Walk, and it is worth copying. “For my part, I like to begin every day, before lifting my head from the pillow, by saying, ‘Thou art within, O Spirit of Christ, though I feel Thee not.’” It is a small thing, and it sets the whole day on the right foundation: a fact believed, not a feeling waited for.

And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed. MARK 1:35

To this he joined the practice he urged in his address on the Spirit: to ask, before leaving one’s room in the morning, to be filled afresh. The still hour was not only for listening and asking. It was for receiving.

When water stands

Why does stillness matter so much? Meyer’s answer in the address In the Secret of His Presence is one of his loveliest pictures. The Spirit within and the presence of God around cannot be discerned, he says, while our senses are busy and our pulse is racing and our minds are full of hurrying thoughts. “It is when water stands that it becomes pellucid,” and shows the pebbles on the bottom. Be still, and know that God is within you and around you.

Be still, and know that I am God. PSALM 46:10

And so his rule: “Let no day pass without its season of silent waiting before God.” He was not asking for hours. He was asking for regularity, for a season kept against the rush.

Carrying the presence out

The still hour was not meant to be shut up in the morning. Meyer wanted his readers to carry God’s presence into the day. He admired Brother Lawrence, the lay brother who worked in a monastery kitchen and claimed to be as aware of God among the pots as at the sacrament. In Our Daily Walk he urges his readers to practise the presence of God: in business or in the midst of daily toil, to lift the heart for a moment into the atmosphere of His presence, and to say to themselves when irritated or worried, the Lord is at hand.

Thou art near, O LORD; and all thy commandments are truth. PSALM 119:151

He recommended one practice that surprises modern readers. Cultivate the habit, he says, of speaking aloud to God as to a present friend, whether sitting in the house or walking by the way — talking over your letters, your plans, your mistakes and your sorrows with Him. “One cannot talk long with God aloud without feeling that He is near.”

And he insisted that the presence is found in work as well as in withdrawal. The place of prayer would lose its light, he says, if we lingered there after the bell of duty had rung below. As we go out to our daily tasks, the angel of His presence meets us at the door and walks beside us.

Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy presence from the pride of man: thou shalt keep them secretly in a pavilion from the strife of tongues. PSALM 31:20

Reading him with care

Meyer liked to hold up examples of unbroken communion — Brother Lawrence, who said he did not lose the sense of God’s presence for more than sixty years, or Spurgeon, who was reported never to pass a quarter of an hour without a sense of the Lord’s nearness. Such examples can inspire. They can also crush, and some sincere Christians who have never known anything of the kind have concluded that something is wrong with them. Meyer’s own teaching on fact and feeling is the best answer: God is present whether we sense Him or not. The still hour is kept not in order to produce a feeling, but because He is there.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Set a fixed time for a still hour — even fifteen minutes — each morning this week, before the day’s business begins. Keep it when you least want to.

2. Try Meyer’s first words of the day before you lift your head from the pillow: Thou art within, O Spirit of Christ, though I feel Thee not.

3. Read Scripture before you pray. Take one verse and turn it into a prayer.

4. Walk while you pray once this week, Bible in hand, speaking to God aloud about your plans and worries.

5. Choose a phrase — the Lord is at hand — and say it to yourself at three moments of irritation or anxiety during the day.

A PRAYER
Lord, my days are full, and I have let the still hour slip away. Forgive me.
Meet me in the morning before the day begins, and speak to me through Your Word.
Let the water of my heart stand still long enough for me to see that You are here.
Then go out with me into the work of the day, and let me find You there too. Amen.
