fields.title: How to Bear Sorrow
fields.body_html:
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me. PSALM 23:4

Meyer was a pastor for more than half a century, and he sat by a great many deathbeds and in a great many darkened front rooms. His address How to Bear Sorrow, in The Secret of Guidance, opens not with a doctrine but with a description, and it is so exact that it can only have come from long listening. You are always listening for footsteps that do not come, he writes, waiting for a word that is not spoken. The savings of a life have gone. Health or sight is failing. Or there is the gap left by death, like a clearing in the forest where the woodman has been at work. Will every day be as long as this? Has God forgotten to be gracious?

He does not rush to answer. And when he does, he gives not one answer but several, like a doctor who knows that one medicine will not do for every patient.

Others have walked this road

The first thing he says is that the road has been trodden by myriads. War, oppression, the slave trade, the unnumbered sorrows of women and children — by far the larger part of the human race, he says, has passed through griefs like ours. Jesus Christ Himself walked the path and left His blood on its stones, and the multitude before the throne came out of great tribulation. It is not much, perhaps, to know we are not alone. But it is something.

Do not talk about punishment

The second is a firm pastoral correction. “Do not talk about punishment.” Meyer allows that we may speak of chastening, for our Father deals with us as sons; or of reaping what we once sowed; or of bearing the consequences of other people’s sins. But punishment for our sins was laid on Christ.

But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. ISAIAH 53:5

If God were still punishing us for our sins, Meyer argues, it would mean Christ’s sufferings were incomplete; and if He once began, a lifetime would not be long enough. This single paragraph has probably done more good in sick-rooms than anything else he wrote. Grieving believers very often assume that their loss is God’s sentence on them. Meyer takes that weight off.

The refiner’s fire

Sorrow is not punishment, but neither is it meaningless. “Sorrow is a refiner’s crucible,” he writes. Whatever its source, once God has permitted it to reach us it becomes His appointment, and He uses it to search and purify. We think we are wholly God’s until the fire shows us, as it showed Job, how much dross there is and how little patience.

And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver. MALACHI 3:3

And God keeps the fire in His own hands. The Father is the husbandman, and His hand holds the pruning-knife; His eye watches the crucible; He will not let even the devil have his own way with us. In The Way Into the Holiest Meyer adds that affliction becomes chastisement when we see the Father’s hand in it. So long as we look only at second causes — at the people and the circumstances — we swing between anger and despair. When we see that nothing can reach us except by His permission, we can smile through our tears. The cup may seem to be mixed by Judas, but it is the cup the Father gives.

The cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it? JOHN 18:11

Tears are allowed

For all his talk of the will, Meyer was no Stoic. “Tears are natural. Jesus wept.” A thunderstorm without rain is dangerous, he says; the rain cools the air. To bear sorrow with dry eyes and a stolid heart may suit a Stoic but not a Christian. There is no need to rebuke the heart that cries for the touch of a vanished hand.

Jesus wept. JOHN 11:35

What matters, he says, is not whether we feel resigned but whether the will is right. People would say to him that it was bad enough to bear their grief, but worse that they could not feel resigned. His reply, he says, was always the same: “You probably never can feel resignation, but you can will it.” Christ in Gethsemane did not feel like drinking the cup. He chose His Father’s will. So Meyer counsels the sufferer to go apart and say, deliberately and repeatedly, whenever the pain comes back: Thy will, not mine. Not because you feel it, but because you will it. And a calm will follow, which is not the absence of suffering but a peace that walks in the midst of it, as the three young men walked in the furnace.

Do not shut yourself away

His next counsel is one many grieving people need to hear. The temptation of great sorrow, Meyer says, is to withdraw, to sit alone and keep silence. Do not yield to it. When a friend wrote to him in the first shock of bereavement to say he must give up his Christian work, Meyer wrote back at once urging him not to, “because there is no solace for heart-pain like ministry.” Sorrow turned inward becomes a Dead Sea, full of salt, beside which nothing grows. Sorrow turned outward becomes the power to comfort others.

Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God. 2 CORINTHIANS 1:4

He goes further. Some trials, he believed, are permitted for no other reason than that we may afterwards help those who pass the same way. So watch each symptom of the pain and each remedy of the great Physician, because one day you will need them for someone else.

The afterward

Finally, Meyer bids the sufferer count on the afterward. God will not always be ploughing. You will one day see the wisdom of His choice, and discover that the thing you wanted was second best. Sorrow is a school; do not leave it without learning its lessons. And the way of the cross, rightly borne, is the only way to the everlasting light.

Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby. HEBREWS 12:11

Reading him with care

In his chapter on chastisement Meyer says that those who suffer most may be heaven’s favourites, and that those who escape the rod should ask whether they are born again. The first can comfort; the second can wound, and neither should be pressed. Scripture does say that the Father chastens every son, but it does not teach that the amount of our suffering measures His love, and a comfortable Christian is not thereby shown to be a false one. Read him on sorrow for his tenderness and his good sense, which are great, and let Job’s comforters remind you that explanations offered too quickly are seldom a kindness.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. If you are grieving, stop calling it punishment. Read Isaiah 53:5 slowly and let the weight go.

2. Say Meyer’s prayer deliberately, whenever the pain returns: Thy will, not mine. Do not wait to feel it.

3. Resist the pull to withdraw. Keep one small piece of service going this month, or take one up.

4. Think of someone passing through a sorrow you have known. Write to them, or visit, this week.

5. If you are comforting someone else, resist the urge to explain their suffering. Weep with them instead.

A PRAYER
Father, I did not choose this sorrow, and I cannot feel resigned to it. But I choose Your will.
Thank You that my punishment fell on Christ, and that this cup comes from Your hand and not from chance.
Keep me from shutting myself away. Let my grief make me gentler with others.
And bring me, in Your time, to the afterward, and to the peaceable fruit of righteousness. Amen.

Do not talk about punishment The second is a firm pastoral correction. “Do not talk about punishment.” Meyer allows that we may speak of chastening, for our Father deals with us as sons; or of reaping what we once sowed; or of bearing the consequences of other people’s sins. But punishment for our sins was laid on Christ. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. We think we are wholly God’s until the fire shows us, as it showed Job, how much dross there is and how little patience. And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver. Scripture does say that the Father chastens every son, but it does not teach that the amount of our suffering measures His love, and a comfortable Christian is not thereby shown to be a false one. Say Meyer’s prayer deliberately, whenever the pain returns: Thy will, not mine. Do not wait to feel it. 3. Resist the pull to withdraw. Keep one small piece of service going this month, or take one up. 4. Think of someone passing through a sorrow you have known. Write to them, or visit, this week. 5. If you are comforting someone else, resist the urge to explain their suffering. Weep with them instead. A PRAYER Father, I did not choose this sorrow, and I cannot feel resigned to it. But I choose Your will. Thank You that my punishment fell on Christ, and that this cup comes from Your hand and not from chance. Keep me from shutting myself away. fields.title: Stripping for the Race
fields.body_html:
Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us. HEBREWS 12:1

Meyer was never content to leave his readers comfortable. After the great roll-call of faith in Hebrews 11, he pictures the heroes of the old covenant rising from the arena into the crowded tiers of a vast amphitheatre, looking down on those of us still running. And then comes the word he loved to press: run. Not sit still and be carried by the stream, not stroll like children coming home from a summer walk, but run, with the concentration of someone who means to finish.

Drifting

He knew that the great danger for most Christians is not open rebellion but a slow slide. In his chapter on the second of Hebrews he takes the epistle’s warning — lest at any time we should let them slip — in the sense the Revised Version gives it, lest we drift away. For every one who deliberately turns his back on Christ, he says, there are hundreds who drift. “It is the drift that ruins men.”

Therefore we ought to give the more earnest heed to the things which we have heard, lest at any time we should let them slip. HEBREWS 2:1

He draws three portraits. A young man from a godly home never renounces his father’s God; he simply finds himself among colleagues who care nothing for religion, relaxes a little, and drifts until he is not sure he ever saw the shore. A businessman who was once upright gives way on small points under the pressure of competition, and the current carries him further than he ever meant to go. A professing Christian stops opening the Bible, not in a single leap but by yielding a little at a time. Meyer’s test is simple. Are you conscious of effort, of daily resistance to the stream around you and within you? If not, you are drifting.

Weights and sins

To run, you must be unencumbered, and here Meyer draws the distinction for which this chapter of The Way Into the Holiest is best known. There are sins, and there are weights. A sin is wrong always and for everyone. But “a weight is something which in itself or to another may be harmless, or even legitimate, but in our own case is a hindrance and an impediment.”

This is liberating and searching at once. Liberating, because it forbids us to judge one another: what is a weight to one is not to another, and each must decide for himself. Searching, because it leaves no hiding place in the plea that a thing is not actually wrong. Meyer asks whether there is anything in your life that takes the edge off prayer, that rises before you in your best moments with a sense of unease, that you would rather not look at closely. It may be a friendship too engrossing, a habit that saps energy, a pastime or a way of reading that absorbs too much. If so, it is likely enough a weight.

Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain. 1 CORINTHIANS 9:24

He anticipates the objection that such stripping will leave life poor. Not so, he answers: the inner life “grows by surrender, and waxes strong by sacrifice.” The athlete gives up much that others enjoy for the sake of a prize he may never use. And God, Meyer says at the end of the chapter, never takes anything from us without giving something better.

The besetting sin

Meyer offers an interpretation of the besetting sin that many readers will not have met. It is usually taken to mean each person’s particular weakness. Meyer argues from the context — the long praise of faith in chapter eleven and the word wherefore that joins it to chapter twelve — that the sin which clings so closely is unbelief. If that is right, he says, unbelief is no longer a mere infirmity to be pitied, but a sin to be repented of.

He is careful to allow for honest doubt. Unbelief may spring, as in Thomas, from real intellectual difficulties, and such doubt keeps praying and stays among believers. But he thought much of the unbelief of his day had moral roots: the soul gets wrong with God and then says it is not sure there is a God. His counsel is practical. Put away known sin. Read the Bible even while you doubt it. Wait. Pray. Live up to the light you have.

Where the thread was dropped

In the address Where Am I Wrong?, Meyer gives the same searching counsel in more personal form. He imagines a conversation with a Christian who has had no conscious joy for years. Did you once have it? Yes. Was there some clear command of God you refused? And the answer comes slowly: yes, years ago, and after a while it faded from the mind. That, says Meyer, is where you went wrong, and you will not get right until you go back to the place where you dropped the thread of obedience and do the thing God asked.

If ye love me, keep my commandments. JOHN 14:15

It is a hard word, and a true one. But Meyer balances it in the same address with a warning against the opposite error. Some Christians, he says, bring darkness on themselves by endless self-examination, forever going back over their motives and their past consecrations. “We must not spend all our lives in cleaning our windows,” he writes, or in wondering whether they are clean, but in sunning ourselves in God’s light, which will soon show us what still needs to be cleaned.

Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: and see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting. PSALM 139:23–24

Looking unto Jesus

The race is run, in the end, not by staring at weights but by looking at Christ. Look off unto Jesus, Meyer urges — away from past failure and success, away from praise and blame, away from the coins scattered on the track — and acquire the habit of looking up from every task to His face, as someone living by Lake Geneva looks up again and again to the snowy mountains across the water.

Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. HEBREWS 12:2

This, he says, is the only way souls are really persuaded. Argue with people about their weights, and they will cling to them tighter. Show them Jesus, and the weights begin to fall away, as snow slides from the branches when the sun comes out.

Reading him with care

Meyer’s reading of the besetting sin as unbelief is possible, but not certain, and the reader should not be troubled by preferring the older view. More important, his suspicion that most unbelief has moral roots is sometimes true and sometimes cruel. Many honest doubters are not hiding a sin, and they deserve patience, not a diagnosis. Meyer allowed for this; the reader should allow for it more generously still.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Apply Meyer’s test: are you conscious of daily effort against the current, or are you drifting? Be honest.

2. Ask the Spirit to show you one weight — not a sin, but a hindrance. Name it, and decide what to do with it.

3. Is there a command of God you once refused and have since forgotten? Go back to the place where you dropped the thread.

4. If you are prone to endless self-examination, stop cleaning the windows. Spend your next prayer time simply looking at Christ.

5. Choose a small reminder to look up to Jesus several times a day, from whatever work you are doing.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, I have drifted more than I have run, and I have carried weights I did not need.
Show me what to lay aside, and give me grace to let it go, trusting that You never take without giving something better.
Take me back to the place where I dropped the thread of obedience.
And keep my eyes on You, the author and finisher of my faith, until I reach the end. Amen.

fields.title: Men of Like Passions
fields.body_html:
Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months. JAMES 5:17

If Meyer is remembered for one kind of book above all, it is the Bible biography. Over many years he wrote a whole shelf of them — on Abraham, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Joshua, Samuel, David, Elijah, Jeremiah, John the Baptist, Peter and Paul — and they were read in homes and Bible classes across the world for generations. None of them is yet in the Ochorus library, so this chapter does not quote them; it describes what he was doing in them, and illustrates it from the books we have.

Mirrors, not monuments

Meyer did not write these books as history. He was not much interested in the questions of date and source that occupied the scholars of his day. He wrote them as portraits of the inner life. What he wanted to know about Abraham or Elijah was how God dealt with a real man — his call, his failures, his testing, his growth — and what that meant for the reader. The heroes of Scripture were for him not monuments on pedestals but mirrors, in which ordinary believers could see their own story and learn what God would do with it.

For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope. ROMANS 15:4

That is why James’s remark about Elijah suits his method so well. Elijah was a man of like passions with us. Meyer loved to show the great figures of the Bible in their weakness, because it put their faith within reach. If God could make something of a Jacob, He could make something of us.

Abraham, the pilgrim

The book on Abraham carries the subtitle The Obedience of Faith, and that is the heart of what Meyer saw in him. Abraham went out not knowing where he was going. In Our Daily Walk Meyer calls him the pilgrim of the unseen, and pictures him stepping out on the wide desert and “only learning his course day by day,” like a sailor on an unknown sea who never knows when the coastline will appear.

By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went. HEBREWS 11:8

This is Meyer’s teaching on guidance in the form of a life. The next step, not the whole road; the cloud followed day by day. And he made the same application every time: the blessing of Abraham is for all who share his faith, and his call is repeated in every believer who leaves the familiar to follow God.

Joseph, the prison and the palace

Joseph was for Meyer the great example of a life shaped by suffering that was not deserved. Sold by his brothers, falsely accused, forgotten in prison, then raised to rule Egypt, Joseph could say at the end that God had meant it all for good. Meyer drew from him the lesson he taught the sorrowing: that God’s hand is in the dark chapters as much as the bright ones. In Our Daily Walk he puts it in a sentence: “God as much sent Joseph to the drudgery and discipline of the prison as to the glory and responsibility of the palace.”

But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. GENESIS 50:20

Moses, the servant

Meyer called Moses the servant of God. Scripture gives Moses forty obscure years keeping sheep in Midian before his call, and Meyer’s whole teaching on waiting under the cloud suggests why such years are no waste. In The Way Into the Holiest he dwells on another side of Moses: the man who went up the mountain in stages, first with the elders, then with Joshua only, then alone into the cloud, and who was shown there the pattern of the true tabernacle. Moses was the servant because he was first the friend who spoke with God face to face.

By faith he forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king: for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible. HEBREWS 11:27

Elijah under the juniper

Meyer’s book on Elijah was subtitled The Secret of His Power, and in The Secret of Guidance he points to the prophet’s own words before Ahab, that he stood in the presence of God. But the scene that drew from him one of his kindest remarks was not Carmel but the juniper tree. After the strain of the contest and the flight from Jezebel, Elijah lay down in the desert and asked to die. Meyer notices, in The Secret of Guidance, that God met that request “not with rebuke, but with food and sleep.” Exhaustion is not apostasy, and God knows the difference.

But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree: and he requested for himself that he might die. 1 KINGS 19:4

Paul, the servant of Jesus Christ

Meyer’s life of Paul carried the subtitle A Servant of Jesus Christ, and he treated the apostle as the supreme example of the surrendered life — the bond-slave who counted all things loss. In Our Daily Walk he follows Paul to Troas, where one door after another had been shut and the little band stood facing the sea, and draws from it his teaching on closed doors and the small opening that leads to a great work. And he recalls how God waited until Paul had given up all confidence in his own strength before He whispered that His grace was sufficient.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. 2 CORINTHIANS 12:9

Reading him with care

The Bible biographies are warm, vivid and often wise, and their very vividness is their danger. Meyer fills the silences of the text with imagined thoughts, feelings and scenes, and he does it so well that a reader can come away remembering Meyer’s Abraham rather than Moses’s. He sometimes draws spiritual lessons from details that will not bear their weight, and like most devotional writers of his day he reads the stories almost wholly as lessons for the individual soul, with less attention to their place in the great story of redemption. Read his biographies with the Bible chapter open beside them, and let the text correct the portrait wherever they differ.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Choose one of the five figures in this chapter and read his story straight through in Scripture this week.

2. Which of them is most like you — the pilgrim, the prisoner, the servant, the exhausted prophet, or the man with the thorn? Why?

3. Look back over a dark chapter of your own life. Can you say yet, with Joseph, that God meant it for good?

4. If you are exhausted, do not mistake it for spiritual failure. Eat, sleep, and let God meet you as He met Elijah.

5. Get hold of one of Meyer’s Bible biographies and read it alongside the Bible text, noticing where he adds to the story.

A PRAYER
Lord, You made great servants out of men of like passions with me. Make something of me.
Give me Abraham’s obedience, Joseph’s patience, Moses’s hidden years with You, Elijah’s prayer, and Paul’s surrender.
When I lie down under the juniper tree, meet me with bread and sleep rather than rebuke.
And write Your story in my ordinary life, for Your glory. Amen.

fields.title: Whom Will You Neighbour?
fields.body_html:
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body. HEBREWS 13:3

It is possible to read Meyer’s devotional books and never guess that their author spent much of his working life among prisoners, drunkards and the destitute. The books are full of the secret place, the still hour and the inner life. But Meyer did not see any tension between the two. The same surrender that gave Christ the last key gave Him the use of the hands and the feet. The God who led the soul into the secret of His presence led the body to the gaol gate.

Holiness in the ordinary haunts of men

He said so plainly in The Way Into the Holiest, in the chapter where he set out his rules for the holiness movement. True saintliness, he wrote, must be natural. The saint who cannot play with children, who looks askance on the great movements of the world and shuts himself up in cloistered seclusion, has missed the pattern of Christ, who watched the children at play in the market-place and sat at the dinner tables of rich and poor alike. “The saintliness of the true saint must find its home in the ordinary homes and haunts of men.”

Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world. JAMES 1:27

In The Secret of Guidance he makes care for others the last of his five cautions for the devout life, and he puts it as a law of the kingdom. “No life can be blessed which is self-centred.” The Dead Sea is walled in and dead. “The secret of having is giving; of learning is teaching; of climbing to the throne is by stooping to wash the feet of the disciples.” And in his address on the secret of God’s presence he warns that the place of prayer itself will lose its light if we linger there after the bell of duty has rung below.

The next person who needs help

The clearest statement of his social teaching comes in a reading from Our Daily Walk on the law of Leviticus 19, and it begins with a definition that clears away a great deal of evasion. “Our neighbour is the next person who needs our help, man, woman, or child.” It is enough, he says, that your help is needed and that you are near.

Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves? And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise. LUKE 10:36–37

The lawyer who asked Jesus that question, Meyer observes, was looking for someone to neighbour him. Jesus turned it round and asked, in effect, whom will you neighbour? Those who go through life waiting to be neighboured, he says, will find it full of disappointment; those who set out to neighbour others will not lack friends in their own hour of need.

What he draws from the old law is strikingly concrete. Leave a margin of your income and produce for those in need. Do not keep back what you owe; he wished all Christians would pay small shopkeepers promptly, and thought it would work a quiet revolution. Be gentle and considerate with those who suffer any infirmity; become eyes to the blind and ears to the deaf. Do not flinch from rebuking sin, but first take the beam from your own eye. And do not bear a grudge.

Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour, neither rob him: the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning. LEVITICUS 19:13

Weld yourself to a life

Meyer did not want his readers to be vaguely benevolent. In the reading on surrender in Our Daily Walk he gives a counsel that sums up his own practice: “Weld yourself to some life or lives that sorely need help. That is what Melbourne Hall in Leicester became under him. He is remembered for going to the prison gate on the mornings when men were released, offering them breakfast and a fresh start, and setting up small enterprises to give them honest wages and a character to show an employer. The work was humble and unglamorous, and work of that kind is never without its disappointments. But he learned there what he taught for the rest of his life: that the gospel of the indwelling Christ is meant to reach the man who has nothing but the clothes he walked out in.

In London the same conviction took him into public life. In Lambeth, among some of the poorest streets in the capital, he campaigned against the brothels and public houses that preyed on the people of his parish,. He was ridiculed for it as a busybody. He kept on, because he believed that loving your neighbour sometimes means standing between him and those who would ruin him.

Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction. Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy. PROVERBS 31:8–9

The oppressed and the Lord

Meyer never let social concern drift loose from prayer. In a reading on Hezekiah’s cry, O Lord, I am oppressed; undertake for me, he lists the many forms oppression takes — poverty, debt, the fear of unemployment, persecution at home, sickness without hope — and says that all of them may be handed to a faithful Creator who is as willing as He is able. The Christian who works among the poor must bring them to the Lord as well as bring the Lord to them.

Reading him with care

Meyer was a man of his time, and some of his social work carries the marks of it. Victorian philanthropy could be paternal, and its campaigns against vice could shade into policing the lives of the poor while leaving the comfortable untouched. Meyer was better than many on this, and far better than those who did nothing. But the reader who takes up his example should also take up the questions a later generation learned to ask: whether the people we help are treated as neighbours or as projects, and whether we are as eager to change our own habits as theirs.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Who is the next person near you who needs your help? Name them, and do one concrete thing for them this week.

2. Set aside a definite proportion of your income for those in need, if you do not already.

3. Pay what you owe promptly, especially to small traders and those who work for you.

4. Weld yourself to one life: choose one person in real need and commit to walk with them over months, not days.

5. Find out what help exists for prisoners leaving prison near you, and ask how you might support it.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You watched children playing in the market-place and ate with the rich and the poor. Keep my holiness from shutting me away.
Show me my neighbour: the next person who needs my help. Give me grace to go to them.
Weld me to some life that sorely needs help, and let me give not words only but deeds.
And as I work, let me bring the oppressed to You, who are as willing as You are able. Amen.

fields.title: Why Sign the Pledge?
fields.body_html:
It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak. ROMANS 14:21

Tucked among the devotional addresses of The Secret of Guidance, between an essay on fact, faith and feeling and another on burdens, is a piece that surprises modern readers: a straightforward temperance tract called Why Sign the Pledge? It is not there by accident. For Meyer, the campaign against strong drink was not a side-interest but part of the gospel he preached. He had seen what drink did in the back streets of Leicester and Lambeth. He had met its victims at the prison gate. And he believed that a Christian who had surrendered his life to Christ should be willing to surrender a glass of wine for the sake of those it was destroying.

The ruin he saw

It is hard now to picture the scale of the drink problem in Victorian and Edwardian Britain. Public houses stood on almost every corner of the poorer districts. Wages were drunk on the way home from work. Wives and children went hungry, and violence in the home was common. Meyer writes with the anger of a man who had seen it close up. There is not a house, he says, in which its slain cannot be found, nor a newspaper that does not record its outrages.

Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise. PROVERBS 20:1

He speaks too of how it creeps up on the moderate. You have no intention of becoming a drunkard, he tells his reader; you scorn the thought. But you take it now for the sake of company, and you may come to take it for its own sake. Wise men, good men, strong men have been mastered by that thirst who no more expected it than you do.

His reasons

The tract is a list of reasons for signing the pledge of total abstinence, and they are a mixture of the spiritual and the thoroughly practical. It is a public protest against a great evil. It will benefit your health and save your time and money; he liked to tell those who signed his pledge cards that there was a banknote hidden inside. It will keep you from temptation. It gives a clear starting point to a new life. It makes a strong obligation, a double knot on a resolution. And it gives you an answer that ends the argument when others press you to drink.

But his weightiest reasons are about other people. If only reformed drunkards signed the pledge, he says, it would become the badge of the reclaimed, and those who most needed it would be ashamed to sign. So respectable people should sign it too, to lend it their good name. And we are creatures of example. “More eyes are watching us than we think.” The boy, the companion, the servant may be waiting to see what we do.

Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend. 1 CORINTHIANS 8:13

That is the ground on which Meyer’s case is strongest, and it is Paul’s ground. A Christian may freely give up a lawful thing for love of a weaker brother. Meyer adds that the temperance pledge had done too much good to be despised now. “We must not kick away the ladder by which we have climbed up.”

God helping me

The heart of the tract is not in its arguments but in three words printed on most pledge cards of his day. “GOD HELPING ME. These words are the heart of all.” A pledge resting on human strength alone, Meyer says, is not worth much. But when a man lifts his heart to God, divine power pours in; a garrison is placed inside the weak nature to hold it against the enemy.

For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil. 1 JOHN 3:8

For those who had signed and broken the pledge, perhaps more than once, he has no scorn. Take it again, he says, in humble dependence on the Saviour. Ask the Lord Jesus to forgive the past, to save you from your enemy, to shield you in the day of battle, and when the door is nearly battered in, to set His foot against it. Put yourself into His hands before you leave your room in the morning, keep looking to Him all day, and praise Him each night. He tells of a working man who was overheard muttering at his bench and explained that he was saying over and over, Lord help me, because it was the only way he knew to keep down his thirst.

Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy. JUDE 1:24

And he adds one piece of advice that shows the pastor behind the campaigner. Avoid the places where drink is sold, he says. “Refuse to enter them unless the Good Shepherd sends you there to find a lost sheep.” The Christian may go into the public house, but only on a rescue mission.

Reading him with care

Here more than anywhere the reader must hold Meyer’s cause and Meyer’s argument apart. His cause was noble. Drink ruined millions in his day and ruins many in ours, and the Christian who chooses total abstinence for love’s sake — for his own weakness, his family, or those who watch him — is following Paul. Meyer’s care for the drunkard, and his refusal to despise the one who fails and tries again, are wholly admirable.

But Scripture does not forbid wine. It warns against drunkenness again and again, and it also speaks of wine that makes glad the heart of man, of a Lord who turned water into wine at a wedding, and of an apostle who told Timothy to take a little for his stomach’s sake. Abstinence may be a wise and loving choice; it is not the law of God, and it must not become a test of Christian standing. Meyer’s tract sometimes leans that way, and some of his health arguments rest on the medical opinion of his time. The reader should keep the love that moved him and leave the overstatement.

For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another. GALATIANS 5:13
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Consider honestly whether alcohol, or any other habit, has more hold on you than you would like to admit.

2. Ask whether your freedom in this area might cause someone close to you to stumble. Would love lead you to give it up, at least in their company?

3. If you have made a promise to God and broken it, make it again in dependence on Him: God helping me.

4. Pray by name for someone you know who is struggling with addiction. Ask whether there is some practical help you could give.

5. Examine whether you have ever judged another Christian by a rule Scripture does not make. Repent of it.

A PRAYER
Lord, You have seen the ruin that drink and every other bondage bring, and You came to destroy the works of the devil.
Give me the love that will give up a lawful thing for the sake of a weaker brother, and keep me from making my choices into laws for others.
For those I know who are in chains, I pray: set Your foot against the door, and keep them.
And in every temptation of my own, let me say and mean it: God helping me. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do. JOHN 17:4

Fifteen chapters can make it look as though F. B. Meyer taught a great many things. He taught one thing, and the rest is that one thing lived out. Our power and peace lie in being where God would have us be — and we are brought there, and kept there, by a Saviour who has opened the way to God and a Spirit who fills the surrendered.

Follow it through and the whole shape appears. Guidance is God making plain where He would have us be, by His Word, His Spirit and His providence, one step at a time. Waiting under the cloud is refusing to go where He has not led. Consecration is giving Him the last key so that He may lead us at all. Fact, faith and feeling put our standing on His work and not our moods. The indwelling Christ and the fulness of the Spirit are the life by which the surrendered walk. The way into the holiest and the great High Priest are the ground of it all. Rest is ceasing from the burdens He never gave us. The still hour is where the day is set. Sorrow is the refiner’s fire in the Father’s hand. The race is run by laying aside weights and looking to Jesus. The Bible biographies show all of this in the lives of men of like passions. And the prison gate, the slum and the pledge card are where it goes when it leaves the closet. One thread, one Lord, one surrendered life.

The danger of this book

If you have read this far, you are in some danger, and Meyer would have named it first. It is possible to read about surrender, guidance and the fulness of the Spirit and turn them into a new ladder to climb, measuring oneself against a crisis one has not had, a joy one does not feel, a sense of God’s presence one cannot keep. Meyer knew the danger. He warned against those who go from convention to convention with notebooks, hungry for the blessing and forgetting the Giver. He told the anxious to stop examining their faith and look at God’s faithfulness. He told the introspective to stop cleaning their windows. And he insisted that the Spirit’s fulness is not a trophy but a daily dependence.

But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. JAMES 1:22

So the plainest counsel this book can give is to go back to the chapter that made you least comfortable, not the one you liked best. Take its application points and work them slowly. Then take the next.

First, give Him the last key. Whatever else you forget, remember the ring of keys and the one held back. If you cannot give it, confess that you are willing to be made willing, and let Him take it. Everything else in Meyer’s teaching waits on that.

Second, go to the gaol gate. Meyer would not be satisfied with a reader who finished this book with a richer inner life and the same closed hands. Find your neighbour — the next person who needs your help — and weld yourself to that life. The still hour and the back street belong together, or neither is what it should be.

We have been honest about his limits. The Keswick language of a second crisis must be read with his own correction, that the filling is sought again and again. His prose can be sentimental, and his illustrations sometimes pile up until the point is lost. His polemic against priests was unkind. His temperance teaching sometimes leaned towards making a wise choice into a rule. And his Bible biographies fill the silences of Scripture more freely than the text allows.

None of this has been said to diminish him. It has been said because he would have wanted it said. A man who taught that consecration must be humble, and that the tone in which some speak of their holiness shows how far they are from it, would not want to be praised beyond the truth.

3. Name the key you still hold back, and pray about it daily for a month.

4. Keep a still hour, however short, every morning for thirty days.

5. Choose one of Meyer’s own books from the Reader’s Guide that follows, and begin it this week.

Take the last key. Lead me where You would have me be, and keep me there.
Fill me each morning, and send me out each day to someone who needs You.
And as You were faithful to Your servant F. B. Meyer to the end, be faithful to me, until we meet in the morning. Amen.

fields.title: A Reader’s Guide to F. B. Meyer
fields.body_html:
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. 2 TIMOTHY 2:15

Meyer is easy to read and easy to find. He wrote for ordinary believers, in short chapters full of pictures, and nearly all of it is now in the public domain. The difficulty, as with most prolific Victorian preachers, is quantity: he published a great many books and booklets, and he repeats himself freely. The guide below is arranged to save the reader time.

Begin here

The Secret of Guidance. A small collection of addresses — on guidance, the loss of Christian joy, Christ’s indwelling, fact, faith and feeling, burdens, sorrow, the presence of God, the fulness of the Spirit, and a temperance tract. It is the best single entry point, and most of this volume draws on it. In the Ochorus library.

Our Daily Walk. A reading for every day of the year, each with a text, a short meditation and a prayer. The readings vary in weight, but the best are among the most practical things he wrote. In the Ochorus library.

On Hebrews and the way to God

The Way Into the Holiest. His exposition of the Epistle to the Hebrews, a chapter to a theme, and the doctrinal foundation beneath his devotional books. Read it for the veil, the blood, the great High Priest, the gospel of rest and the race; read it with care where it turns to controversy. In the Ochorus library.

On the inner life

The Shepherd Psalm, a gentle exposition of Psalm 23; The Present Tenses of the Blessed Life, on what the believer may have now; Christian Living, a collection of short practical addresses; The Directory of the Devout Life, on the Sermon on the Mount; Tried by Fire, on the First Epistle of Peter; and Love to the Uttermost, on the closing chapters of John’s Gospel. Our Daily Homily, a large set of short readings through the whole Bible, was one of his most used books. None of these is yet in the Ochorus library.

The Bible biographies

Abraham, or The Obedience of Faith; Israel, a Prince with God, on Jacob; Joseph, Beloved, Hated, Exalted; Moses, the Servant of God; Joshua and the Land of Promise; Samuel the Prophet; David, Shepherd, Psalmist, King; Elijah and the Secret of His Power; Jeremiah, Priest and Prophet; John the Baptist; Peter, Fisherman, Disciple, Apostle; and Paul, a Servant of Jesus Christ. These are the books for which he is best remembered. Begin with Elijah or Abraham, keep the Bible open beside them, and notice where he fills the silences of the text. None is yet in the Ochorus library.

Approach with care

The chapters of The Way Into the Holiest that deal with the Christian priesthood contain sharp polemic against Roman and Anglican priests; take the argument from Hebrews and leave the tone. Why Sign the Pledge? pleads a noble cause but leans towards making abstinence a rule for all, and its health arguments are dated. His Keswick addresses on the fulness of the Spirit and the surrendered life are best read alongside his own insistence that the filling is to be sought daily and that there was more in the doctrine than he had grasped.

About Meyer

W. Y. Fullerton, F. B. Meyer: A Biography (1929), written by a friend and colleague soon after his death, is the standard older life; warm, anecdotal and admiring. Ian M. Randall, Spirituality and Social Change: The Contribution of F. B. Meyer (1847–1929) (2003), is a careful modern study that takes his social work and his Keswick spirituality together, and is the best place to see the whole man. Bob Holman’s F. B. Meyer: If I Had a Hundred Lives is a shorter and more popular account by a writer with his own long experience of work among the poor. The Ochorus author page carries a shorter biography.

Three counsels for reading him

Read him with the Bible open. Meyer claimed no authority of his own and would be the first to send you to the text. Check his applications against it.

Read him for the substance, not the upholstery. His illustrations can be many and his prose sentimental. Look past them for the plain counsel underneath, which is usually sound and often searching.

And read him with your hands open. Nearly every reading he wrote ends in a prayer, and nearly every address ends in a call to do something before evening. Pray the prayer, and do the thing. A chapter obeyed will do more than a shelf admired.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21
